title: LangSmith BYOC is now available on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud
summary: LangSmith BYOC now runs on AWS (GA), Azure and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, and agent deployments stay in your cloud account while LangChain runs it.
story_key: story|title:langsmith byoc is now available on aws azure and google cloud
content_excerpt: LangSmith Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) now runs on AWS (GA), Azure (Beta), and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, datasets, prompts, and agent deployments stay in your own cloud account, on the cloud you choose, and LangChain manages the data plane for you, from orchestration and scaling to platform updates. By splitting the control plane and data plane in two, BYOC provides greater flexibily to decide where agents run and where telemetry lives, without taking on the work of running LangSmith. LangChain runs the control plane , which holds auth, org and workspace config, billing metadata, hashed API keys, and static UI assets. You own the data plane , which holds everything sensitive, from traces, prompts, and datasets to experiments, agent deployments, and workspace secrets. An organization can hold several data planes, each in its specific account and region, and each data plane holds its workspaces. This lets you split data planes by region, environment, or business unit. For example, a platform team might run production and staging data planes in separate AWS accounts, while a business unit that standardized on Azure runs its own, separate BYOC deployment on Azure. Each team's traces land in the account that team owns. Until now, teams with strict compliance boundaries deployed and maintained self-hosted LangSmith. This kept their data inside their own boundary, but it took dedicated platform engineers to patch stateful services, configure databases, and run schema migrations. With BYOC, LangChain provisions and operates LangSmith inside your own virtual network. Consider a team running agent applications across several environments. With self-hosted, every update to the execution components meant coordinating downtime and managing custom Helm rollouts in each environment. With BYOC, the data in your data plane stays in your VPC while LangChain handles scaling, schema updates, and runtime dependencies. While self-hosting continues to be a reliable deployment option for customers who require complete control, BYOC provides the best of both worlds for customers who need it. Since we launched BYOC on AWS in August, many teams have chosen to run LangSmith in their own cloud with BYOC. They point to three main benefits: By expanding LangSmith BYOC to Azure and Google Cloud, more teams can get access to this experience while choosing their preferred cloud vendor. Each cloud has its own network policies, identity model, and security requirements, so BYOC

title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts
summary: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.

title: AutoCompress: Automated Hardware-Guided Model Compression
summary: LLM pruning must preserve quality while meeting hardware- and workload-specific constraints on latency, throughput, and memory. Existing pruning workflows often target parameter counts, requiring practitioners to manually select model sizes that meet latency, throughput, and GPU memory limits. However, parameter count alone does not predict these metrics, which depend on the model architecture, workload, hardware, and serving engine. We introduce AutoCompress, a hardware-guided compression framework that directly incorporates such constraints into differentiable architecture search. AutoCompress jointly optimizes global and per-layer structure to produce heterogeneous architectures, guided by serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end latency, throughput, and memory measurements. We evaluate AutoCompress on long-context local coding, batched datacenter serving, and latency-sensitive in-game interaction. Compared to the state-of-the-art Minitron pruning framework, AutoCompress improves average accuracy across eight benchmarks by 6.57, 2.35, and 0.57 percentage points on RTX 5070, RTX 5080, and H100, respectively. AutoCompress also compresses Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters for single-B200 BF16 serving at 128K context, retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score.

title: SpecCTMC: Exact Speculative Simulation of Diffusion Language Model Continuous-Time Markov Chains
summary: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel text generation, but independently sampling multiple tokens can disrupt their dependencies and change the output distribution. Exact continuous-time sampling avoids this approximation, yet typically requires one sequential model evaluation per token. We introduce SpecCTMC, a training-free speculative sampler that reduces this sequential bottleneck without a separate draft model. SpecCTMC proposes successive token updates using previously computed model predictions, evaluates their intermediate states in parallel, and applies an exact acceptance-and-correction procedure. We prove that SpecCTMC preserves the joint distribution of event times, generation order, and token values of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain. It therefore introduces neither time-discretization error nor additional factorization error from parallel decoding. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B across five benchmarks demonstrate 1.73-4.38x fewer sequential model evaluations than direct continuous-time sampling, while preserving the reference sampling distribution. Our code is available at: https://github.com/kasakh/specctmc

title: How We Optimized Browser Use for Deep Agents
summary: We compared seven browser toolsets for Deep Agents, picked Stagehand from Browserbase, and tuned it with LangSmith traces and evals. Here's what we learned.
story_key: story|title:how we optimized browser use for deep agents
content_excerpt: Browser agents can now take on multi-step work that's painful and time-consuming for people. Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse plan cross-country road trips, cancel unused subscriptions, and list cars for sale, all on sites with no public APIs. DataDome saw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone. Browser use helps in two places: actions an API can't cover, like using a website the agent wasn't set up for, and end-to-end testing of the web apps coding agents build. Either way, the agent needs two things: This post focuses on the tools, and on making them good enough that the agent uses the browser well. We set out to give agents in Managed Deep Agents a browser. We compared seven toolsets and picked the best one, Stagehand ( GitHub ) from Browserbase . Then we improved it based on what agents did in LangSmith traces, and validated every change with evals. The biggest lesson was how much room there is to improve an agent through tool design. Browser use toolsets come in a few forms: native tools, an MCP server , or a CLI the agent runs in a shell. Browser use poses two unique challenges for those tools: We iterated with the agent development lifecycle : run the agent on a benchmark, read its traces in LangSmith to see where it wasted steps or tokens, change the tool, and run evals to check that the change helped. Every run was a LangSmith experiment , so we could compare setups side by side and click from any number into the trace behind it. We had every harness return structured output (a JSON answer). That way a formatting slip, like a one-line reply to a task that asks for a table, didn't count against its browsing. We upstreamed that option to Browserbase's evals. We first held the model and tasks fixed and changed only the toolset. The seven toolsets differ in how the agent calls them: Every toolset passed between 78% and 90% of tasks, but cost and speed varied widely. The Stagehand tools passed the most (90%) for $1.98 in total, at a median 17.4 s per task. Playwright MCP passed 78% for $26.71, about 13x the cost, and took three times as long per task ( full results ). The gap held on harder tasks. On HardBench's 38 core tasks, Deep Agents passed 30 with Stagehand's code-writing run tool and 21 with Browserbase's command-style browse CLI, at three times the cost per task. Early browser tooling repurposed testing SDKs like Playwright . As Browserbase puts it, "Playwright was built for testing, we built Stagehand for your agent

title: Introducing Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for vLLM and Kubernetes
summary: Kinference is a new open source inference control plane for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM and Kubernetes, providing token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies.
story_key: model:vllm|title:introducing kinference an open source inference control plane for vllm and kuber
content_excerpt: We’re excited to announce Kinference [kay-inference] , a new open source project for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM. We created Kinference at Buoyant after watching our customers struggle to run open weight models in their environments. We designed Kinference to be the control plane layer for the platform you need to build. It uses vLLM to do the underlying inference, and provides the set of features necessary for building an inference platform in practice. This includes token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies. Kinference can be paired with your existing stack. Using Kinference is simply a matter of pointing inference clients to its HTTP endpoint and sending OpenAI or Anthropic-compatible inference traffic there. Kinference serves a heterogeneous, evolving set of models running on a heterogeneous, evolving pool of GPUs, to a heterogenous, evolving set of clients.. In addition to policies and a routing layer, Kinference provides inference-specific load balancing that takes into account signals like GPU queue sizes, historical performance, and the contents of the KV cache on the GPU. This KV-cache awareness, in particular, allows Kinference to send requests to the vLLM worker that will do the least work for that specific request. Modeling the KV cache content of the GPU can produce dramatic gains in performance for distributed inference. For example, in our public Kinference benchmarks , we showed that, when compared to standard Kubernetes load balancing (labeled “service” below), Kinference (labeled “kinference”) was able to cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 95% and median end-to-end latency by 45% of requests on one workload type. By incorporating cache awareness into policies, platform owners can create policies that will send simple requests to the cheaper model — but only if that’s less work than sending them to the expensive model in the first place. In our unloaded latency benchmark above, we sought to measure the effect of Kinference’s KV-cache-aware load balancing in isolation. In our capacity benchmark, below, we measured the requests per minute can each endpoint can serve within a latency SLO. In the capacity benchmark, Kinference served 7.4× the goodput on shared-prefix and about 3.5× the goodput on multiturn . title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
summary:
Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. Yet even benchmarks that are carefully validated at release can become stale. As models improve, they can discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject, while changes to evaluation infrastructure can invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. We call the resulting accumulation of defects benchmark maintenance debt: a growing gap between benchmark scores and the capabilities they are intended to measure. We introduce a continuous-validation workflow for agentic benchmarks that combines community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs. We apply this workflow to Terminal-Bench 2.0, a benchmark that underwent extensive human and LM-assisted review and red-teaming before release. Our audit identifies issues in roughly 30% of the benchmark, and we release the resulting repairs as Terminal-Bench 2.1. These repairs change evaluation results: accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points and leaderboard positions move by up to three ranks, even as the overall ranking remains highly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.958).
  We evaluate how resource allocation shapes benchmark conclusions. We show that fixed wall-clock can materially change agent performance: For example, extending the time limit closes a 20pp harness gap on GPT 5.4 and shrinks a 30 pp gap on GPT 5.4 mini to 5 pp. Benchmark maintenance is therefore not only about repairing task artifacts: resource budgets are part of the measurement specification and must be validated alongside the tasks themselves.
  More broadly, benchmark maintenance debt is not just accumulated implementation bugs: our results show that as models improve, both evaluation assumptions and resource settings may need to be revalidated.

title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
summary: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.

How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies in legal tech history. The team started in a Stockholm basement with ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Today, a lawyer can use Legora to draft and edit Word documents, review 10,000 contracts in a single table, or run due diligence. The agent also coordinates work between lawyers, clients, and other agents. When Legora made its own acquisitions, the team used it for diligence. • Why Legora resisted adding a model picker for years, and why it finally added one • Jacob’s estimate that models already do about 60% of legal work well, and why the rest takes a smarter model • How three engineers and three lawyers build test environments modeled on customers’ work, much like the “worlds” used in reinforcement learning • A citation problem where the model got it right 70% of the time, then 99% after one release. Legora didn’t have to change anything. • Tabular Review, the million-cell spreadsheet the industry copied down to the name • How intake works, how agents create lists, and how a list can start another agent • What legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers each do, and who gets to write code • The 300 Spartans slide Jacob used to argue that 20 engineers would be enough forever. summary:

title: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
summary: Genie 4: our new world model unlocking unprecedented realism in real-time simulation.
story_key: story|title:genie 4 a new generation of world simulation
content_excerpt: Today, we are announcing Genie 4, our new world model, which unlocks unprecedented realism and improves real-time interactive simulation. Genie 4 is natively multimodal, enabling audio-like music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue to be simultaneously generated with the world. The Genie 4 model incorporates and builds on capabilities from the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors the simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models provide the complex reasoning needed to help maintain a simulation’s coherence and continuity. With this foundation, you can set an event in motion, and Genie 4 simulates what happens next: how the world responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move, react, and speak. Understanding and simulating the world is a crucial aspect of building AGI. Genie 4 advances our ability to create safe, infinitely variable simulations that can help with everything from developing training environments for robots and agents to unlocking the creation of new interactive experiences. We have started rolling Genie 4 out as a research preview for trusted testers — gathering feedback before we release it to consumers and developers, starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie here . Genie 4 delivers enhanced photorealism, fluid movement, and native audio. All accompanying sounds featured above are produced directly by Genie 4. The following are recordings of real-time interactions from Genie 4, where users use standard keyboard controls for navigation and camera control, and text prompts to steer the scene as it evolves. With Genie 4, you can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time — like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object — and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene. Between your inputs, Gemini also monitors and steers the scene to keep the world progressing cohesively. Prompt: Use the reference image as the exact first frame and visual basis for the scene. Preserve the same floating rectangular platform, weathered concrete edges, wild grasses, ferns, twisted small tree, warm glowing amber sphere, and the same middle-aged man in a loose brown suit playing a brass saxophone. title: claude-code v2.1.318
summary:
What's changed

  • Added a record of your answer when Claude Code asks to turn on the mods it writes in a session
  • Added assume_role on mantle upstreams of the Claude apps gateway, for a role in another AWS account and for per-developer AWS cost attribution
  • Added an effort option to a mod's $.model.fork, so a quick side job can run at low whatever effort the session uses; the result reports the effort sent
  • Added the date a stored claude.ai sign-in ends to claude auth status (loginExpiresAt) and to claude -p JSON results (credential_expires_at)
  • Added a one-line stderr warning to claude -p text output, starting 10 days before a stored claude.ai sign-in ends
  • Fixed --continue sometimes losing the earlier conversation after a malformed tool call's retries ran out (regression in 2.1.314)
  • Fixed macOS sessions with many running Bash commands stalling while memory grew
  • Fixed permission prompts being answered by keys typed just after sending a message, or before a slow prompt appeared
  • Fixed /logout, claude auth logout and claude mcp remove reporting success, and changes to trust, consent or MCP settings being dropped with no word, when the config file could not be updated on a shared network home directory
  • Fixed jobs exiting with Not logged in when another terminal or host signs in again to the same account and organization on the same home
  • Fixed claude mcp add and remove writing the config without its lock: they now wait for it or exit 1, though another job's save can still replace a saved server
  • Fixed claude plugin commands exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
  • Fixed claude plugin validate passing a custom-named marketplace file that claude plugin marketplace add rejects
  • Fixed stdio MCP servers that exit on the version probe being re-probed on every start; a server that dies in under 3s for its own reason is also pinned to the legacy handshake for 7 days
  • Fixed sessions being refused at startup by an allowedProviders list that another login on the same machine had stored
  • Fixed idle compaction replacing a conversation with a reply that was not a summary
  • Fixed the "Now using usage credits" notice reappearing about every 30 seconds while a background subagent is running
  • Fixed custom slash commands that fail, or that only Claude can invoke, printing nothing in claude -p and SDK sessions
  • Fixed claude -p and Agent SDK sessions reporting success when an API error cut off a reply while a mod hooked turn.step
  • Fixed a message sent right after a model change still running after Stop in headless sessions: Stop now cancels or stops it as it would a queued message
  • Fixed a deleted session transcript being re-created with its last prompt when an idle non-interactive session exited
  • Fixed claude remote-control hosts, the background daemon and self-hosted runners failing to start new sessions (spawn ENOENT) after an update or version cleanup removed the binary of a still-running process
  • Fixed a running Claude Code process owned by another user (for example one left by sudo claude) being treated as dead by version cleanup, which could delete its binary
  • Fixed /remote-control showing a session as available after a failed connection
  • Fixed /design revoke reporting success when the request failed with a 404
  • Fixed a shell command approved after a self-hosted runner or cloud session restart running in the session's start folder, not the folder it was asked in; if that folder can't be entered, it is not run
  • Fixed Claude not being told when an approved connector tool was unavailable after a cloud session restart
  • Fixed cloud sessions being stopped in the middle of a turn when the service refuses uploads for several minutes
  • Fixed variables a Setup hook writes to CLAUDE_ENV_FILE not reaching the Bash tool in some cloud sessions
  • Fixed the iPhone app showing a cloud session's turn as finished while it kept running, after a response was cut off at a tool call or a refused image or document was removed
  • Fixed a restarted session re-sending a message that failed with an API error, ahead of the newer message waiting behind it
  • Fixed a restarted session dropping its interrupted turn when the restart came right after Claude read a large image or retried a tool call
  • Fixed every connection failing when the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS file is empty, not PEM, or starts with a damaged certificate: readable certificates are now used, with a warning on stderr
  • Fixed workflows re-running finished agents when resumed after a usage limit
  • Fixed /mcp in cloud sessions counting tools the model can't use; a server's row now shows how many of its tools are available
  • Fixed a duplicate notification when Claude left the status field out of a PushNotification call
  • Fixed the error for a too-large image in a request with more than 20 images always saying the limit was 2000px; it now shows the API's limit
  • Fixed the runtime in background shell details not updating while the dialog is open
  • Fixed a mod's turn.step hook making a stopped reply finish as a success in headless runs
  • Fixed retention cleanup leaving a home that only runs claude -p with no ~/.claude.json backup: it now takes a fresh backup before deleting the last good one
  • Fixed the stored login being replaced by an empty file when a network home directory has no room left for data but still takes new files
  • Fixed tokens from setup-token being refused at start on machines with forceLoginOrgUUID, when the token belongs to a permitted organization
  • Fixed non-interactive launches replacing a ~/.claude.json that isn't valid JSON with defaults; the start now fails, says how to restore the file, and leaves it as is (#87551)
  • Fixed an empty ~/.claude.json with no backup being reported as corrupted; Claude Code now starts as it does when the file is missing
  • Fixed the restore command printed for a damaged or missing ~/.claude.json naming an empty or cut-off backup, or failing on a read-only file
  • Fixed the sign-in failure when a stored claude.ai login reaches its time limit: it now says so, and in claude -p names claude auth login and claude setup-token
  • Improved how ~/.claude.json, settings files and the stored login survive saves on shared network home directories: they are less often deleted, briefly emptied or replaced by a near-empty or older copy
  • Improved sessions on network file systems to look again when the configuration file is wrongly reported as missing, so fewer start without your MCP servers and trusted folders
  • Improved MCP tool errors: a call made before the tool is loaded now returns its input schema
  • Improved the reliability of git commits and pull request creation when the Bash tool runs macOS's built-in /bin/bash
  • Improved "Ask your admin for more usage" in the usage limit menu to send the request in one step
  • Improved how fast remote sessions reconnect after a pause or sleep
  • Improved You should know toasts to say "try again" instead of "press 2", which only works in the terminal
  • Improved auto-update reliability: a brief network failure while verifying a release is now retried right away instead of waiting for the next check
  • Improved unattended runs (claude -p, SDK apps) to stop rewriting ~/.claude.json on every run when nothing in it changed
  • Changed Claude Code to no longer install or update the IDE extension when started in an IDE terminal; use /ide from an outside terminal or your editor's extensions view
  • Changed subagents to stop instead of switching models when "Switch models when a message is flagged" is set to "Ask each time"
  • Changed background subagents to move a shell command to the background after 3 minutes on all providers, so the prompt cache doesn't expire while it runs
  • Changed subagent progress summaries on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, or with telemetry off: on a cold prompt cache, one can now wait up to 5 minutes for the subagent's pending response
  • Changed what a mod attaches at prompt.submit to stay in the user's turn rather than go out as a system message
  • Changed deniedMcpServers URL entries to also block Anthropic-provided servers whose upstream URL matches, and connectors in cloud sessions and on self-hosted runners, where the session is given the connector's own URL; otherwise deny a connector by name
  • Changed the /permissions rule details, built-in rules and delete confirmation views to use the standard dialog; pressing Ctrl+C twice there now goes back or cancels instead of quitting
  • Changed /claude-api managed-agents-onboard to give a new agent's built-in tools, and a quickstart template's MCP tools, the auto permission policy ("Judge risky actions") by default, matching the Claude Console; say "run without asking" to opt out
  • Removed the 2.1.288 fix that kept the model's earlier thinking when resuming a conversation started on 2.1.286 or earlier; that thinking can now be dropped
  • Gateway: Added a log warning when the Google access token from a federation (external_account) credentials file is about to expire
  • Gateway: Improved the log hints about listen.trusted_proxies: they now say to list only a proxy that adds the connecting address to X-Forwarded-For itself
  • Gateway: Improved the warning when AWS CountTokens fails on Amazon Bedrock: it says Claude Code, not the gateway, counts after the 501, and points at IAM only when AWS denies access
  • Self-hosted runner: Added CLAUDE_RUNNER_SPAWN_REASON to the orchestrator's spawn-runner hook environment: why Anthropic sent the request (e.g. runner_lost, resumed); unset when none was sent
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a startup warning when --release-idle-session-min is the last argument with no value (still ignored) or has a value of only spaces (still read as 0)
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the orchestrator's log lines: ok session=… now prints at every log level on stdout (was debug only, stderr) with reason=… after jti=…, and nack session=… ends its fields with reason=… after retryable=…; update scripts that match retryable=true: or retryable=false:
  • Remote Control: Fixed a misleading "spawn error: ENOENT" when a session's working folder is missing; the error now names the folder
  • Remote Control: Improved the title a fork of a terminal fork is created with when the app doesn't set one: "Name (fork 2)"
  • [VSCode] Fixed a window whose sign-in the organization's settings refuse starting a new Claude Code process in the background every minute
  • [VSCode] Fixed a long word in the chat panel's error banner pushing its close button out of view
  • [VSCode] Improved the sign-in screen to show what Claude Code printed when its sign-in status check fails
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a No repository option: a cloud session on an Anthropic-hosted environment can now start without picking a repository
  • [Cloud sessions] Added the usual Chrome names to cloud sessions, so tools other than Playwright can find the built-in Chromium through google-chrome and CHROME_PATH
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a New session button to the card shown when a cloud session's environment was deleted, where the message box is hidden
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed reading GitHub Actions logs in cloud sessions: gh run view --log and gh api log requests now get the log in most environments, not an unreachable redirect
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved most Create PR failure messages in cloud and Remote Control sessions: they now give the reason or a link to GitHub instead of saying Try again
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed connector search results to tell Claude that the search covers only part of the connector directory
  • [Remote Control] Fixed side-by-side checkouts of one repository looking identical in the environment menu's Remote Control rows; each now shows its own folder name
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed keyboard focus and screen reader announcements in Claude Tag admin setup; pressing Escape in the connect form no longer also closes the Add dialog
  • [Code Review] Improved the Code Review analytics page to retry once after a server or network failure, then show a Try again banner instead of empty cards
release_highlights: Added a record of your answer when Claude Code asks to turn on the mods it writes in a session
Added assume_role on mantle upstreams of the Claude apps gateway, for a role in another AWS account and for per-developer AWS cost attribution
Added an effort option to a mod's $.model.fork , so a quick side job can run at low whatever effort the session uses; the result reports the effort sent
